trade: History class in the union hall's meeting room — learner and oral history volunteer
header: Lower-secondary history at a union hall's meeting room: how to record an oral history interview with a retired worker, from consent and open questions to listening, checking and archiving, with the interviewee invented for the lesson and memory treated as a source to be weighed like any other.
name: Oral History Interview Skills
tagline: Ask consent, ask open questions, then listen — a memory is a source, not a verdict

badge.name: Careful Listener
badge.note: An interview recorded with consent, open questions and follow-ups, and the memory weighed as a source

hazards.label: Start recording before asking permission?
hazards.text: You started recording before asking permission. An oral history belongs to the person telling it; they decide whether they are recorded, what is kept and who may hear it. Consent comes first, every time, and it can be withdrawn.

hazards.label: Ask a question that tells them what to say?
hazards.text: You asked a question that suggested its own answer. A leading question puts your idea into their memory and makes the recording less trustworthy; open questions like how, what and tell me about let them say what they actually remember.

hazards.label: Treat the memory as proved fact?
hazards.text: You wrote the memory down as a proved fact. Memories are precious evidence of how things felt and what mattered, but they change over time; a historian checks them against other sources, just as they would a document.

hazards.label: Post a clip online without asking?
hazards.text: You wanted to post a clip online without asking. The interviewee agreed to a class archive, not the internet; sharing beyond what they agreed breaks their trust and their consent. Ask first, and respect the answer.

find1.title: Find what you need before the interview
find1.cue: Mark the three things you need ready before the interview begins.
find1.why: A good interview is prepared. A consent form sets out what will be recorded and who may hear it, a short list of open questions keeps the conversation focused without controlling it, and a working recorder means the words are kept. With those three ready, you can give your full attention to listening.
items: It records what the interviewee agrees to.
a short list of open questions
Open questions let them tell it their way.
Check it works before, not during.
decoy: A striking thing to ask about later, but not something you need ready to start.

select1.title: Ask for consent before recording
select1.cue: Explain what the recording is for and ask the interviewee to agree before you press record.
select1.why: Consent is the foundation of oral history. Explaining clearly what the recording is for, who will hear it and that they can stop at any time lets the interviewee make a real choice, and it is how every responsible archive works.
select1.label: Ask for consent first

seq.title: Put the interview in order
seq.cue: Consent, an easy opening, open questions with follow-ups, then thank and check.
seq.why: Consent first makes the interview possible. An easy opening, such as asking where they grew up, helps the interviewee relax. Open questions and follow-ups draw out detail, and a thank-you with a check of what they are happy to share closes it respectfully.
seq.oon: Out of order. Consent comes before anything is recorded.
items: start with an easy opening question
ask open questions and follow up
thank them and check what may be shared

hold.title: Hold the pause while they think
hold.cue: Stay quiet and hold the pause while the interviewee gathers their thoughts.
hold.why: The best part of an answer often comes after a pause. Staying quiet and letting the silence sit gives the interviewee time to remember, instead of jumping in with another question that cuts off what they were about to say.
hold.brk: You filled the silence too soon. Let them think, and hold the pause again.
hold.label: Hold the pause

turn.title: Turn the recorder's level to their voice
turn.cue: Turn the recording level so their voice is clear without distorting.
turn.why: A recording that is too quiet loses words, and one that is too loud distorts them. Setting the level to the interviewee's voice before the main questions means their words will be heard clearly by everyone who listens later.
turn.label: Recording level

gauge.title: Check the voice level is in the band
gauge.cue: Commit when the level meter sits in the band as they speak.
gauge.why: A level meter shows whether the voice is being recorded well. Checking it while they speak, not only in silence, catches a quiet speaker or a noisy room before the whole interview is spoiled.
gauge.label: Voice level
gauge.miss: Outside the band. Adjust the level before the main questions.

drag.title: Choose an open follow-up question
drag.cue: Drag the open follow-up card into the question slot.
drag.why: A follow-up like tell me more about that invites detail in the interviewee's own words. Choosing it over a yes or no question keeps the story theirs, and it is the single most useful habit of a good interviewer.
drag.label: Tell me more about that
drag.miss: Not in the slot yet. Put the open follow-up in the next question.

select2.title: Say how a memory is a source
select2.cue: Say what a memory can tell a historian, and what it needs checking against.
select2.why: A memory tells you how something felt and what mattered to the person who lived it, which documents often miss. But memories change, so a historian checks the details against records and other accounts, weighing the memory as they would any source.
select2.label: Memory as evidence

find2.title: Spot the problems in a classmate's interview plan
find2.cue: Look at the draft interview plan and mark each problem.
find2.why: Interview plans go wrong in familiar ways: no consent step, leading questions and a plan to share recordings more widely than agreed. Spotting them helps you plan an interview that is both good history and respectful of the person.
items: a question that suggests its answer
a plan to post clips online
decoy: Thanking the interviewee is good practice. Keep it.

track.title: Keep listening through a long answer
track.cue: Keep your attention on the speaker through a long answer, noting follow-ups quietly.
track.why: Long answers are where the richest stories are, and staying attentive through them shows respect as well as catching details worth asking about. Noting follow-ups quietly lets you return to them without interrupting the flow.
track.brk: Your attention wandered. Bring it back to the speaker.
track.label: Listening held

record.title: Record the archive notes
record.cue: Write who was interviewed, when, what they agreed to and a summary.
record.why: An archive note tells future listeners what the recording is and what they may do with it. Writing the consent terms beside the summary protects the interviewee and makes the recording useful for years.
record.label: Archive notes

share.title: Thank the interviewee and check the sharing
share.cue: Thank them and confirm what they are happy for the class archive to keep.
share.why: Closing with thanks and a check of what may be kept respects the gift of their story. It gives them the last word on how it is used, which is at the heart of every ethical oral history project.
share.label: Thank and check

checkin.title: Check in at the end of the session
checkin.cue: What did the interview teach you that a book could not? What was hard?
checkin.why: A check-in gives learners a chance to reflect on what they heard, which may have been moving, and to say what they found difficult about interviewing. It is not marked, and the teacher or a trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk.
checkin.label: End-of-session check-in

interrupts.label: Pause and offer to stop
interrupts.alert: The interviewee's voice catches while describing a hard time at work, and they look upset.
interrupts.cue: Pause the recording and gently offer to stop or take a break.
interrupts.why: An interviewee's wellbeing matters more than the recording. Pausing and offering a break or an end gives them control, and it is what every oral history guide asks interviewers to do.
interrupts.miss: You pressed on with the next question, and the interviewee ended the session upset.
interrupts.wrong: That carries on regardless. Pause and offer to stop. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Recording paused, a break taken. The interviewee chose to carry on.

interrupts.label: Say what the consent covers
interrupts.alert: The oral history volunteer asks what the interviewee agreed to and who may hear the recording.
interrupts.cue: Say what the consent form covers and who may hear it.
interrupts.why: The volunteer is checking you know the limits of consent. Saying exactly what was agreed shows the recording will be used only as the interviewee wished.
interrupts.miss: You were not sure, and the volunteer had to check the form before anything could be kept.
interrupts.wrong: That does not say what was agreed. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Consent terms stated. The volunteer files the recording.

guide.after: A memory is a source to weigh.
guide.hazard: Stop. Did they consent? Is the question open?

lateRecord: The archive notes are written once the interview is over — nothing to record yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the session.
